articles.headline: I tried Windows 11’s customizable right-click menu – and it’s a much-needed change
keyFacts: Microsoft released a new customizable right-click menu for Windows 11 in the Insider Beta preview to reduce clutter and disorganization.
Users can add, remove, and rearrange commands, apps, and file actions through File Explorer or the Windows Settings menu.
The new menu could officially debut for all Windows 11 users before the end of the year, depending on Insider feedback.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- The new customizable right-click menu is now available for testing.
- You can add and remove entries in the menu to reduce the clutter.
- The new menu could officially debut before the end of the year.

The right-click menu in Windows seems like a great idea. Quickly access different commands, settings, and apps by right-clicking a folder, file, or other item in File Explorer or on your desktop. But as you install more applications, the menu gets more disorganized and difficult to navigate.

With Windows 11, Microsoft revamped the menu with a smaller and simpler layout. But this approach doesn’t work well either, as it often excludes commands and apps you frequently use. With another mouse click, you’re able to view the older-style menu, but that brings us back to the original problem.
More from ZDNET
How to try Windows 11’s new customizable right-click menu

With the latest Windows 11 Insider Beta preview, you can try out the new customizable menu for yourself. You’re able to add or remove specific commands. You can move certain items to different spots. And you can include entries for certain actions, such as editing a text file with Notepad or opening an image in the Photos app. The goal is to reduce the clutter and confusion of the current menu.

To try this yourself, you’ll need to join Microsoft’s Windows Insider Program if you haven’t already done so. Choose the Beta channel and then just download the latest updates. Since these Insider builds can be unstable, don’t set this up on your primary PC. Instead, use a spare computer, a dual-boot setup, or a virtual machine. I run the Insider builds in a VM through VMware Workstation Pro.

With the latest update installed, open File Explorer and right-click on a folder or file. You’ll now see a new entry to customize the menu. Select that to tweak the context menu. Otherwise, go to Settings, select Personalization, and then click Context menu.

First on the list, you can turn certain file actions on or off, such as Send to, Print, Create shortcut, Copy as path, and Rotate image. As always, the actions that appear are context-sensitive. So, the command for Rotate image appears only if you right-click an image file.

Next, you can choose which apps pop up all the time, either in the main menu or in a submenu. These include Copilot, Clipchamp, Notepad, OneDrive, Paint, and Photos. But the list will also incorporate any third-party apps you install, so you can easily decide whether or not they should appear.

Finally, under additional options, you can choose to display the standard file commands (Cut, Copy, Paste, Rename, Delete) either at the top of the menu or within the menu. You can elect to put cloud-storage actions in their own section, show the Customize menu command in the menu itself, and move the Properties command to the bottom of the menu. You’re also able to display a command to show more options, which displays the old-style menu.

“We’re rolling out an updated context menu experience in File Explorer, designed to feel faster, cleaner, and easier to tailor to the way you work,” Microsoft said in an article about the latest preview build. “The new design reduces top-level clutter, keeps commonly used actions easy to access, and adds a new Settings experience that gives you more control over what appears in the menu. As we continue refining this experience with Insider feedback, our goal is to make right-click feel more responsive, predictable, and personal.”
A much-needed change

I’ve been trying the new menu, and it certainly offers a much-needed change to the otherwise cluttered and complicated right-click menu. However, I’d like to see Microsoft eventually get rid of the kludgy old-style menu completely. Otherwise, you’re still stuck with the dual-personality approach that gets in the way of using the current menu more smoothly.

Since the new customizable menu is currently in the Beta channel, it’s one step closer to its official debut. That time frame will depend in part on the feedback from Windows Insiders. To share your own thoughts about the feature, open the Feedback Hub in Windows and select the My Feedback option. If the overall feedback is positive, we could certainly see the new menu reach all Windows 11 users before the end of the year.

articles.headline: Kylian Mbappé apologises after being dropped by Chinese brands for Mao Zedong comment
keyFacts: Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé apologised after being dropped by major Chinese brands for joking about Mao Zedong in a viral video.
Major Chinese brands including Dongpeng, Mengniu, and Milkground terminated their partnerships with Mbappé following the incident.
State-run media reported that Chinese public television suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches and removed advertisements featuring Mbappé.
body: Kylian Mbappé has apologised after the Real Madrid forward was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral. There were also signs of broader repercussions, with the state-run Chinese digital newspaper The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from La Liga.

The offending video shows Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen involving him was of his face photoshopped on to that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao.

“My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone my words have upset,” Mbappé said in a statement in French, Chinese and English.

Spain’s La Liga also apologised, saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga.” In China, jokes about Mao, the country’s founding leader who died in 1976 – and whose drastic policies are also blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths – remain taboo.

The beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year’s World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé consuming its sport drink, said it was terminating all cooperation with the France captain. “Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” Dongpeng said in a statement.

Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, and cheese maker Milkground also said that they were cutting ties with Mbappé, who until now was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of social media followers. “Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappé” was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo with 430 million views.

One Weibo user said the “extremely serious wrong remarks … crossed the red line” and others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappé’s image from their bottles. Dongqiudi, one of China’s biggest online football outlets, said Mbappé’s remarks were “offensive to China and the Chinese people”.

In an interview with the French sports newspaper L’Equipe last month, the 27-year-old Mbappé addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator. “There’s a part of it that’s funny … but there is another part that’s a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history,” he said.

China’s foreign ministry said it was aware of the reports regarding Mbappé, who on Monday finished runner-up to Harry Kane in the Ballon d’Or award for the world’s best player. “Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with unanimous rejection from all sectors of Chinese society,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.

The Paper cited sources at the state broadcaster saying that CCTV has suspended all broadcasts of La Liga matches, and removed all advertisements involving Mbappé. On the CCTV website, La Liga matches this weekend were still on its online viewing schedule.

Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there. The former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island’s then vice-president and current president, Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media. Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.

The Houston Rockets general manager, Daryl Morey, posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to China suspending sponsorship deals with the NBA and pulling games off Chinese television for a year.

Fans in China made their feelings clear. “I used to really enjoy watching Mbappé play on the pitch,” Zhang Jingqi, 30, who works at a mall in Beijing, said. “But ever since this news broke yesterday I have lost that admiration, sorry to say.”

articles.headline: Mao, memes and Mbappé: Chinese brands drop soccer star in fury over ‘dictator’ joke
keyFacts: Several Chinese brands and platforms cut ties with soccer star Kylian Mbappé after he referred to Mao Zedong as a dictator during an interview.
The backlash led to apologies from both Mbappé, who called his comment ill-judged, and La Liga, which distanced itself from the remarks.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun stated that words hurting the feelings of the Chinese people will face a collective boycott.
body: HONG KONG — He’s one of the world’s most popular athletes, but Kylian Mbappé is suddenly paying the penalty for being on the wrong side of China’s fervent nationalism.

The French soccer star’s own goal? Suggesting that Mao Zedong, the founding leader of communist China, was a dictator, in comments that revolved around memes portraying Mbappé as an authoritarian figure.

A host of Chinese brands said Tuesday that they were cutting ties with the French captain, the latest example of how rapidly celebrities can go from having their faces plastered in subway stations and on drink bottles to drawing condemnation over political sensitivities that are little understood outside China.

The scale of the backlash prompted La Liga, the Spanish league of which Mbappé is the leading light, to apologize and distance itself from his remarks. Mbappé himself then apologized “to everyone my words have upset,” saying that his “comment was ill-judged.”
The swift apologies aimed to head off what had been a wave of outrage.

Dongpeng Beverage, known for its energy drinks, Inner Mongolia Mengniu Dairy, one of China’s largest dairy producers, and cheesemaker Milkground all issued similarly worded statements early Tuesday announcing that they were terminating their ties with Mbappé.

The Chinese social media platform Xiaohongshu also distanced itself from Mbappé, saying its contract with him had ended after he appeared in a 2024 ad for the platform that went viral. On Tuesday, a note on Mbappé’s Xiaohongshu account, which had more than a million followers, said it had been suspended “for violating community guidelines.”

The companies did not specify Mbappé’s missteps, but the statements came after a clip circulated widely on social media Monday showing an interview last spring with the French online talk show “The Bridge.”

Mbappé is often depicted jokingly online as a dictator because of his outsize presence on and off the field. Fans have created memes comparing him to a number of authoritarian historical figures, including Mao.
In the clip, Mbappé was asked which meme was his favorite.
“A video someone made of a guy… I think he was a Chinese dictator,” he said. The clip then shows Mbappé’s face superimposed on an image of Mao, whom Mbappé did not mention by name.
His comments drew fury in China, where he was accused of insulting a country that has been a lucrative source of income for him.

“Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with a collective boycott by all sectors of Chinese society,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Tuesday at a regular briefing in Beijing.

Foreign athletes have run afoul of Chinese sensitivities in the past, sometimes with profound economic consequences for major sports leagues. NBA games were largely suspended from Chinese broadcast for years in 2019 after a Houston Rockets manager expressed support for anti-government protests in the Chinese territory of Hong Kong, and in 2023 former NBA star Dwight Howard drew controversy when he referred to the Beijing-claimed island of Taiwan as a country.
According to a commentary Tuesday by Global Times, a state-backed nationalist tabloid, sporting events and advertisements involving Mbappé have also been suspended from broadcasting.

“Mbappé is not an isolated case. He has now paid the price, and deservedly so,” the commentary said. “His experience should serve as a clear red line for all foreign public figures seeking to enter the Chinese market.”
After reports that broadcasts of the Spanish league, where Mbappé plays for Real Madrid, had been suspended in China, the league distanced itself from the remarks.

“We deeply regret” the comments “that have caused discomfort and offense in China,” La Liga President Javier Tebas said in a post on social media. “We cannot allow an individual’s action to tarnish” La Liga and its clubs’ relationship with China, Tebas said, adding that it was working with its partners in China to “overcome the situation.”

In his own apology, also posted to social media, Mbappé said that “during a recent interview, I reacted to an image of myself. My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world.”
He added: “I apologize to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry.”
Mbappé came a close second Monday for soccer’s prestigious Ballon d’Or award.

He has criticized the dictator memes in the past, telling the French sports newspaper L’Équipe last month that while he knew they were meant to be humorous, they also showed “a lack of political and human awareness.”
Mao has a deeply mixed legacy in China, which he led for more than a quarter-century until his death in 1976.

In 1949, Mao’s communist forces won China’s drawn-out civil war, unifying the country after a century of foreign invasion and domestic turmoil. In the decades that followed, Mao oversaw sweeping reforms that included the “Great Leap Forward” — a radical industrialization campaign that contributed to famines that are believed to have killed tens of millions of people — as well as the “Cultural Revolution,” a violent anti-capitalist movement that stirred political and social chaos for the last decade of his rule.

China’s ruling Communist Party has acknowledged Mao’s role in those events but maintains that his achievements outweigh his mistakes. His stature within the party remains high, and his portrait appears on the 100-yuan bill, the largest denomination of Chinese currency.
Mao also continues to be a source of inspiration for some young people frustrated by China’s slowing economy and fiercely competitive society, and Mbappé’s comments drew online criticism.

Many didn’t know what exactly Mbappé had said, however, given China’s strict censorship controls.“I don’t care what exactly he said. If it was insulting to China, then it hurt my feelings. I support boycotting him,” read one comment on Weibo.

Mark Dreyer, author of a book on China’s sports industry, said the episode was the latest involving China in which a story fuels outrage that forces brands to take action to protect commercial interests no matter the context or truth.

“The ultimate result is that sports stars and global celebrities will become increasingly cautious about engaging with China,” Dreyer said. “It’s hard to see how this outcome benefits China or its sports fans in the long run.”

articles.headline: Anthropic could just stop
keyFacts: Anthropic is pursuing an initial public offering for a two trillion dollar valuation while warning that AI could pose catastrophic risks.
CEO Dario Amodei defends the company strategy as a race to the top intended to compel competitors to prioritize safety.
Critics argue that Anthropic is accelerating AI capability development and should consider unilaterally pausing its progress.
body: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says his AI company can drive a “race to the top.” Where’s the evidence? | Finn Gomez/Getty Images

We’re living through an AI-fueled “ Black October ” and things are changing fast. Hackers are using AI to breach countless companies. AI tools have uncovered security flaws that could leave 70 percent of all websites vulnerable. Governments are scrambling to secure their sites . Banks , too. And because cyberhacks can hurt supply chains, some longtime AI watchers are going full prepper , stocking up on food, cash, and more.
In the center of this story is Anthropic, one of the world’s leading AI companies, which was explicitly founded on the promise that it would be a “good guy” company in a world of dubious tech giants.

Anthropic says all the latest developments are very serious. Its security chief wrote last week that things are “going to get a lot worse before they get better.” Two weeks ago the company warned that AI models could soon self-replicate on the internet-connected devices in your home, like smart fridges and robot vacuums. And its co-founder now says “ the singularity ” — when AI systems speed up technical progress in a way that’s hard for humans to comprehend — “is here.”

You might think, given its view of the risks, that Anthropic would be pumping the brakes on its cutting-edge AI progress. Just the opposite. Anthropic filed for a blockbuster initial public offering on Monday, chasing a valuation of $2 trillion even as it warns in the IPO filing that AI could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Every day, it is racing toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) , where AI models are smart enough to build the next, even smarter AI models by themselves.
How does Anthropic justify that?

As its CEO, Dario Amodei, reminded the world last week, he built the company on one big bet: that instead of driving a race to the bottom, where companies skimp on safety in their rush to beat competitors in the market, Anthropic could actually catalyze a “race to the top.”
Why I wrote this story

As I’ve watched Anthropic double down on its “race to the top” strategy, I’ve been uncomfortably reminded of another very risky gambit: Sam Bankman-Fried’s crypto fraud of 2022. There are important differences between the two; this is not a perfect parallel. But both involve a tiny handful of figures, strongly influenced by effective altruism, making huge bets on behalf of many, many other people.

EA culture prides itself on offering a counter to commonsense morality. The community has shown a willingness to take big risks and justify them with complex calculations. Sometimes that pays off . But believing you are intelligent enough to adopt a counter-intuitive, galaxy-brained strategy and end up saving the world with it often involves some hubris. And hubris makes me nervous in a field as high-stakes as AI.

The idea is that if Anthropic proves it can build AI that’s both powerful and safe, the market will expect both — so other AI companies will then feel compelled to compete on safety, too. That may sound nice in theory, but it means Anthropic has to keep building ever-more-powerful AIs.

“The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier,” Amodei wrote . “And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.”
In other words, Amodei is sticking to his bet.

But Amodei is gambling with, by his and his company’s own telling, the future of humanity. If AI goes wrong, it could lead to our gradual disempowerment , a galling concentration of power , or even complete extinction .

So there’s a very basic question that the public deserves a good answer to right at this pivotal moment: What is the evidence that Anthropic’s stated strategy — compete at the frontier so as to drive a “race to the top” — is actually successful overall?

From the outside, it looks like Anthropic has done more, on balance, to drive a race to the bottom. (Disclosure: Future Perfect is funded in part by the BEMC Foundation, whose major funder was also an early investor in Anthropic; they don’t have any editorial input into our content.)

In fact, part of the problem may be that Anthropic continues to treat this as a classic arms race. Specifically, the company seems to model it as a prisoner’s dilemma: If Anthropic stopped building more powerful AI, another player — whether it’s China, OpenAI, or another company — would just build it anyway. In this kind of dilemma, if the other player is going to defect, it’s rational for you to defect, even though nobody actually wants that outcome.
But what if this framing misses the point?

Game theory can make a huge gamble seem sophisticated, while making the obvious alternative — just don’t build a doom machine — seem naive. Yet the fact that Anthropic and others are now racing toward RSI makes it much more likely that we could lose control of AI and start to see massive damage to our world. When the cost of defecting from safety is that you create a serious risk of catastrophic harm — or of all humanity, including you, going extinct — is that still a “rational” move?
Instead of telling yourself that you can galaxy-brain your way through this with fancy enough game theory, maybe you’re better off just thinking of this as something much simpler: Russian roulette.
More and more leading voices in AI are starting to recognize that.

“We should stop AI progress now, starting unilaterally with Anthropic and/or OpenAI stopping — and then broadening out as a second step to more AI companies and negotiations with China,” Geoffrey Irving, who was until recently the chief scientist at the UK AI Security Institute, told me. “Unilateral pauses can’t hold for long, but they are the right first step: When you’re doing a very dangerous thing, the correct action is stop, even if others are also doing dangerous things.”
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.
The case that Anthropic has done more harm than good

Let’s be clear: The question is not whether Anthropic has done anything good on the safety front. It has. Standing up to the Pentagon , temporarily holding back access to frontier models, and publicly advocating for safer AI policies are a few examples, among others .
But the real question is whether the company’s “race to the top” strategy is working on balance — whether it’s net-negative or net-positive for safety.

Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at AI safety advocacy organization Encode, recently set off a firestorm among tech watchers, writing on X, “When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to superintelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary.” Here’s his list of what Anthropic has done:

And this is all just in the past year. If we rewind the tape further back, we see Anthropic pushing back on a landmark bill to regulate AI . Rewind even further back, and we see indications that Anthropic’s core strategy may have been flawed from the start. According to Reuters , in late 2022, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman heard rumors that Anthropic was building an AI-powered chatbot. So he ordered his employees to ship an OpenAI chatbot first. That chatbot was called ChatGPT. We all know the rest.

The rivalry between OpenAI and Anthropic seems not only to have hastened the arrival of generative AI, but also to keep pushing release dates forward to this day. The two companies have been known to release new or cheaper models within hours of each other , each one keen to protect its market share.

Even if you think Anthropic’s behavior was justified in 2022 because publicly demonstrating the risks of AI also demonstrates the need to regulate AI — a common claim within the company and AI discourse writ large — you have to ask: Is it still justifiable now, when AI has reached this level of power and sophistication?

Anthropic has indicated that it’s getting closer and closer to achieving RSI. In January, Amodei himself wrote , “I am concerned that LLMs are approaching (or may already have reached) the knowledge needed to create and release [biological weapons] end-to-end, and that their potential for destruction is very high. Some biological agents could cause millions of deaths.” And he wrote in September, “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet .”
But at this point, Amodei and his staffers are themselves perhaps the primary ones accelerating the rate of AI capability development.

“Anthropic seems to be doing the whole RSI thing more than anyone else, other than perhaps OpenAI,” Calvin told me. “And I just think that seems insane given their publicly stated views on the risks.”

“I think people at Anthropic should reckon more with the fact that it seems like the modal outcome is that the largest impact that Anthropic will have had is dramatically accelerating the race to RSI,” he continued. “On the current trajectory, everything else they will have done and thought and ideals they had will be a rounding error compared to their contribution there.”

Anthropic should be willing to invite scrutiny on this point — and, if it believes it’s actually making the field safer than it otherwise would be, to show us the receipts. How? It could put before Congress a bill that actually strengthens safety, instead of weakening it. It could stick to its former Responsible Scaling Policy and get other companies to do the same, instead of jettisoning its commitments. It could influence other labs not to build RSI, instead of leading the charge.
In the absence of such evidence, the “race to the top” logic just doesn’t hold water.
What if Anthropic just…stopped?
Amodei has begun advocating for “pacing the frontier” of AI development. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote in September.

The catch is that Amodei’s plan to slow down is contingent on others agreeing to slow down too — other AI labs, to start with, and also other countries. But more experts are now saying that it would be better if a frontier company like Anthropic unilaterally stopped.

“I’m glad that he proposed that we pace, but like, now we have to actually do it — and it seems like he’s saying he’s not going to do it unilaterally,” Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI who became a prominent whistleblower , told me. “That’s not very helpful, Dario! You should lead. What’s all this about ‘racing to the top’ and ‘leading by example’ if you’re just waiting?”

Voluntary unilateral action by individual companies is of course no substitute for federal regulation and international treaties. But Irving argues that it’s the right first step, because if the companies wait for governments to rein them in, it may well be too late. Governments are notoriously slow. An individual company can act today.
There’s a perennial objection here: “But China!”
Yet the idea that we’re in a classic arms race with China has always been flawed .

For starters, AI is not just one thing with one purpose, like the atomic bomb. It’s a much more general-purpose technology, like electricity. So what matters isn’t simply who gets it first, but who uses it in which ways. Besides, if the harms from AI are massive, then those harms are relevant for the other party, too. The Chinese don’t want to see catastrophic harms to all of human civilization, either. So we shouldn’t write off the possibility of coordination.

Former Vox reporter Kelsey Piper recently wrote about a colloquium at Anthropic where one participant objected: A decade ago, Facebook considered acquiring the tech that would later power TikTok. But, facing pressure due to privacy and safety worries, the company passed. That didn’t end up protecting us from the scourges of a world with TikTok — all it did was hand China an early monopoly on the tech. Piper writes:
Was this a policy success? Did we want to repeat it?

We were obliged to grudgingly concede that it didn’t sound like a policy success. We did not want to repeat it. China might be no excuse for the U.S. labs to do reckless things, but it is a real consideration.

Our next step might be bilateral talks with China, then. But by the point where you agree that Anthropic’s plans might depend on bilateral talks with China, you’ve already conceded most of the steps of Anthropic’s worldview that seemed so much like madness 10 minutes ago: continue working on AI for now, try to negotiate a slowdown, but don’t abandon work at the frontier and all the advantages that come with it.

But TikTok is not a good analogy for RSI. The former may be a cesspool that rots our brains and amplifies ethnic hatred, but its dangers don’t compare to the dangers of RSI. The TikTok case may indeed be best approached as a classic prisoner’s dilemma. But with RSI, the potential downside is so catastrophic that anyone who proposes to save the world precisely by building the tech that endangers it is making a hell of a gamble on behalf of everyone else. At the very least, the burden of proof should be on them to prove their confidence is justified.

AI insiders often think those outside of their industry can’t possibly understand the technical, geopolitical, and moral complexities they’re facing. But commonsense morality is commonsense for a reason: It tracks intuitions that are usually right (such as, if you don’t want a doom machine, maybe don’t build a doom machine) and trains us to be appropriately skeptical of huge, counterintuitive bets to the contrary.

Precisely because the AI landscape is a complex system — there are so many actors (including different AI companies and different governments), and actions from each can trigger actions from others in ways that are hard to predict — believing you’re smart enough to take highly counterintuitive actions and end up saving the world as a result is an extremely risky gambit. Instead, maybe it’s best to just do the straightforwardly right thing: Stop.

To be clear, “stopping” doesn’t have to mean peeling back everything that’s been done in AI so far. The powerful AI systems that are already out there can’t be put back in the box. And we may need some AI to defend from the AI that’s already out there.

“I’m not saying shut down all of your data centers,” Calvin said. “But I’m saying that in particular, pushing the frontier on RSI and making it so that you’re going to be the company that is doing more fully autonomous development than anyone else in the world, does that actually make any fucking sense?”
Increasingly, both AI insiders and the public are shouting no .

Some insiders, perhaps aware that humanity is perfectly capable of shutting down overly dangerous tech development (we’ve done it before ), are speaking out and quitting jobs at AI companies . At public gatherings, like the recent Pro-Human Assembly in Washington, DC, and the People’s AI Assembly in New York City, people are piling on the pressure to rethink the AI race. States are drawing up their own legislation to rein in the tech . And a single X post from Calvin got so much attention that no less than Amodei himself felt compelled to respond . The AI companies are being forced to pay attention.
Attention may not be all you need, but it’s a start.

articles.headline: The Future of Wet Cat Food Dispensers Is Here. My Review of Neakasa Riko
keyFacts: The CNET reviewer tested the $240 Neakasa Riko, a smart cat feeder that separately stores and rehydrates freeze-dried food using an integrated water tank.
The reviewer found the app intuitive and praised features like removable storage tanks, dishwasher-safe bowls, and a practical mealtime chime.
The reviewer noted that feeding a cat exclusively with freeze-dried food using the device is significantly more expensive than traditional canned food or dry kibble.
body: After a health scare a couple of years ago, my cat spent a while on a wet food diet before I finally got him back to dry food with a smart pet feeder. During that time, I learned how tricky wet cat food can be: You need to serve it fresh, and it can’t sit out too long. Leaving the house meant planning my day around the next meal, spending more than on dry kibble and keeping a steady supply of wet food on hand — canned or otherwise.

Although wet cat food was inconvenient, it was the price of keeping my cat healthy and happy at the time. I looked into automatic wet food dispensers, but most required freezer packs to keep the food chilled, and the few refrigerated models held only enough for a day or so.

So you can imagine my excitement when I learned about the Neakasa Riko, a smart cat feeder that rehydrates food meal by meal. It stores freeze-dried food and water separately — and it’s also somewhat compatible with other dry food. When it’s time to dispense food, it grinds and soaks the food before serving your cat. I spent a month with the Neakasa Riko to see how it might help cat owners. Here’s what I learned.
More from CNET
How the Neakasa Riko makes wet food easier

At first glance, you see right away that the Neakasa Riko is not your typical smart cat feeder. The most obvious tells are the 80-ounce water tank on the right-hand side and the retractable feeding bowl below the food hopper. Because it sits directly below a grinder and water jets on the underside of the dry food storage, the retractable bowl lets food sit long enough to rehydrate before a cat digs in. (I doubt many cats will wait for the food to rehydrate.)

While the Riko specifically targets freeze-dried food, Neakasa notes it may also work for air-dried and baked cat food — but it doesn’t recommend using it with extruded kibble. In addition to freeze-dried food, I tried the Riko with my cat’s regular food: Supreme Source. This brand says you can soften food with water as needed, but I noticed the Neakasa Riko doesn’t grind it at all. Early results are promising — mostly because my cat doesn’t seem to care about the texture — but I’m not ready to let the Riko take over the entire feeding process just yet.

Using a mix of freeze-dried food and kibble with the Neakasa Riko might be a great fit for most cats. A few cat food brands already offer such mixes. You’ll still need to figure out the best water-to-food ratio for your cat, but it’s worth considering. Although it can dispense water separately from food, I don’t think it’s a good use of the unit other than possibly having a secondary water source for your cat after mealtime until the next feeding.

I like that the storage tanks are easy to remove for refilling and cleaning. Helpfully, the unit won’t run without the food hopper’s lid in place, because it’s low enough that most cats could eat food from the hopper rather than the bowl. It even chimes to remind you to put the lid back. As with other smart feeders I’ve used, the Riko has a compartment for desiccant packs to help keep food fresh.

This smart pet feeder comes with two dishwasher-safe stainless steel bowl inserts, making it easier to clean than other smart feeders I’ve used. Interestingly, you calibrate the food dispenser scale with the bowl removed, so you can swap the bowl quickly without recalibrating or zeroing out the scale. It’s a practical solution that keeps your pet’s bowl clean.

My starter kit also included wet wipes to clean the inside of the unit, spare desiccant packs and a limescale cleaner to remove hard water deposits from the water tank. Lastly, there’s an optional rechargeable battery pack, which I didn’t test, but it comes in the Riko Everyday Set. Neakasa claims the battery can provide up to seven days of backup power.
The Neakasa app is good

During my time with the app, I found it fairly intuitive and liked that the Riko’s main tab included useful information, such as daily feeding history, quick access to manual and scheduled feeding controls and estimated food and water levels. While the settings menu has quite a few features — such as feeding controls, reminders, calibration, a child lock and deep cleaning — I like that Neakasa organizes them based on what you’re most likely to use.

I’m generally ambivalent about smart feeders making sounds or having displays, as pets generally don’t need these features to know when food hits the bowl. However, the Riko’s mealtime chime is a helpful reminder for pets that might’ve forgotten the food after it started to rehydrate.

Similarly, the Riko’s small display shows the feeder’s status. When idle, you can also set the display to show a clock, simple icon or custom text. However, the custom text always scrolls, even when it’s short enough to display all at once. I found this movement distracting, so I opted for a simple heart icon instead. Likewise, you can turn the display off entirely or set it to a Do Not Disturb schedule for nighttime — the same goes for the sound settings.

The Neakasa Riko doesn’t integrate with smart home systems. This is understandable, as the main appeal is scheduling feeding times and monitoring pet food intake. While I’m sure that aggregating this information in a platform such as Home Assistant may benefit some power users, other smart home compatibility features — like automating lighting, smart locks and energy tracking — don’t seem important. For example, the only automations I would want with a smart feeder are lights changing color to indicate an error or low food level.
Putting the Neakasa Riko to the test

Switching a cat to a new type of food is usually a long process, as most brands recommend slowly phasing in the new food over many days until they transition completely. Because my cat’s diet is already stable, I didn’t want to subject him to a completely new food paradigm — not to mention the high cost of freeze-dried chicken. As a result, my testing with the Neakasa Riko mostly involved replacing daily treats. This way, I can enrich his existing diet with rehydrated chicken while getting a feel for how the Riko operates.

It took a few feedings to dial in the best water-to-freeze-dried-chicken ratio. I started with equal amounts of food and water, which apparently wasn’t appetizing to my cat, who took most of a day to eat a serving. My concern with this is that I don’t want food sitting out and spoiling. Fortunately, the solution was simply adding more water to each serving. In my case, I found a 1:4 food-to-water ratio was the sweet spot — the cat usually ate everything within a few minutes.

As much as I like that the Neakasa Riko retracts the bowl when too much food remains uneaten, the safety retraction threshold must be 10 grams or higher — you can choose a value between 10 and 60 grams — so it won’t work if you’re feeding only small amounts of food. If you’re dispensing a lot of food, it’s worth testing how much your cat will eat and how quickly.

I don’t recommend leaving your cat home alone with the feeder for multiple meals until you’re sure it can meet your cat’s needs. This way, you can avoid coming home to a hungry kitty because the Neakasa Riko’s food safety feature has kicked in. (You can disable the setting, but leaving wet food out to spoil isn’t worth the risk.)

One quirk I noticed about the Riko is the way it handles scheduling. Notably, each feeding was an hour after my schedule. I’m not sure why — there’s no Daylight Saving Time setting, and my time zone was correct. The fix was easy: I moved the schedule up an hour. While you can adjust the rehydration time for manual feedings, the scheduled ones seem to take about 20 minutes. I like that this provides plenty of time for water to soak in.

Once the bowl is empty, it stays out until the next food or water distribution. At first, I found this behavior perplexing because I assumed the bowl would retract when empty to keep it out of the way. However, I think this is a good feature for two reasons. First, it gives your pet a chance to lick the bowl clean or get the last tiny morsels. Second, it keeps the bowl easily accessible for when you want to swap it for a clean one, something I do whenever I ran the dishwasher.
Is the Neakasa Riko worth it?

The real benefits come from the convenience and improvements to your cat’s quality of life. For $240, the Neakasa Riko fills a useful niche, especially if you want to diversify your cat’s diet with nutritious freeze-dried food or softened kibble. Outside of a few scenarios, my gut says it isn’t a complete replacement for wet food.

To support my intuition, I compared the prices of canned cat food and freeze-dried cat food. The average price per daily serving of freeze-dried cat food — based on a 10-pound adult cat — from brands such as Weruva, Instinct and Stella & Chewy’s is roughly $5.18. That’s nearly five times as much as the $1.05 from budget canned brands such as Friskies and Meow Mix. It’s also $0.90 more than premium canned brands such as Sheba and Fancy Feast, which average $4.28 per serving. While Instinct is more competitive than the premium brands, at $3.67 per serving, you’re still paying $110 a month to feed it exclusively to your cat.

Even premium dry kibble brands are much cheaper per serving. For example, my cat’s food costs about $30 per 11-pound bag and lasts nearly two months at $0.48 per serving. It’s cheaper than most budget canned food, but still pricier than Walmart’s Special Kitty canned food brand ($0.23 per serving) — budget kibble brands offer even more savings. (The cheapest kibble may include added filler that isn’t nutritious — ask your vet for good options that won’t break the bank.)

When you factor in the cost of traditional canned wet food, competing feeders come out ahead on meal costs. The $170 Petlibro PLAF109 uses a simple refrigeration system to keep three meals fresh — Petlibro doesn’t guarantee freshness beyond three days, but this is an excellent compromise for sticking with canned food. If you want up to six meals, the $262 PetSafe FreshFeed can keep them fresh for up to six days. While you can find cheaper smart wet food dispenser designs from generic brands, none seemed particularly noteworthy in my research.
Should you buy the Neakasa Riko?

Setting aside meal costs, the Neakasa Riko is easily the most convenient smart feeder for wet cat food. It holds up to 10 days of meals and uses less energy than refrigeration. Plus, you don’t have to fill individual meal compartments. At $240, it sits comfortably between Petlibro and PetSafe. The Neakasa Riko’s biggest advantage is that it can dispense most kinds of dry pet food, plus freeze-dried food. You can likely get great results with standard dry food, but you may need to settle for moist (or soggy) morsels rather than the soft texture of canned cat food.

It also bridges the gap with standard dry food feeders, keeping Riko as an option for wet or dry food as your pet’s needs change. I think Riko is a better long-term value than the $190 PetLibro Granary Vision 2 I tested recently, mostly because it doesn’t require an expensive subscription. Even without PetLibro’s subscriptions, Riko’s added wet food capability more than justifies the initial price difference. However, on the dry food front, I’m inclined to stick with the $100 PawSync as my preferred smart pet feeder.

There’s certainly a case for choosing the Neakasa Riko, especially if you want an excellent way to manage wet food. Still, using it exclusively with freeze-dried food will strain all but the most robust pet food budgets.

articles.headline: Apple says it will replace iPhone Duo handsets with screen problems
keyFacts: Apple announced it will replace iPhone Duo handsets that have developed screen problems shortly after the device went on sale.
Affected users reported issues including display lines, center crease cracks, and crunching noises when opening the new foldable phone.
Apple stated it is aware of the issue on a small number of devices and urged customers to contact the company.
body: - Published
Apple says it will replace iPhone Duo handsets that have developed problems with their screens just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.
Photos posted on social media show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device, which has a starting price of Â£1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.
Apple said it is aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.
The Duo's launch, which attracted crowds at Apple stores around the world last week, comes as the brand tries to reinvigorate its range of devices and challenge the foldable phones made by rivals.
Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.

An iPhone Duo user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a device with lines across the right side of the display and later uploaded a picture of a new handset alongside the broken one, thanking an Apple store in New York for its help.
The extent of the issue remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, while some images showing faulty devices may have been created using artificial intelligence.

The Duo's 7.6-inch (19.3cm) inner display is held together by a central hinge - a complex piece of engineering that has resulted in similar flaws in folding devices made by some of Apple's competitors.
Samsung's first foldable phone, the Galaxy Fold, suffered an early setback in 2019 when reviewers reported broken screens on the devices.
Android users already have a broad selection of foldable phones to choose from, technology that Apple spent years developing before the Duo's release.
It is Apple's most expensive iPhone ever, costing up to Â£3,199 for the most well-equipped models.
The Duo marks Apple's first major iPhone redesign in almost two decades and was unveiled by new chief executive John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September.
When closed, the Duo looks like a wider version of an iPhone, then opens up to a device resembling a small tablet computer.
"Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together", Ternus told an audience at Apple's California headquarters last month.
The Duo, he said, would "redefine the experience of using a foldable phone".
